The main comparison contains five development pages and five additional pages fixed before their outcomes were inspected. The additional pages reuse the five attack templates in different articles, so this tests sensitivity to surrounding content. A separate developer instruction says that retrieved text cannot authorize additional actions, providing a simpler baseline that requires no activation access.

These controls answer different questions. Zero dose checks whether the machinery itself changes the outcome. Reversing the direction tests whether its sign matters. A second proxy task: selective execution
In a separate earlier experiment, I gave GPT-OSS-20B a page with two harmless file-writing commands, A and B. The page requested both actions; the
permitted only one and asked the model to report the fresh random value in each command. I changed only which action the
permitted. This let me measure unwanted writes, correct completion of the permitted action, and whether the answer used information from both commands.
Without steering, changing permission shifted the probe's scores on both commands together. In all eight available baseline cases, permitting the first-listed action raised both commands' mean
scores. In one example, command B scored 34.27%
when A was permitted and 28.26% when B itself was permitted. The command text and scored token positions were unchanged. A higher mean
score therefore did not consistently identify the permitted command.
The task also showed why I need to measure useful behavior. Across 21 matched comparisons,

steering prevented four unwanted writes and introduced three. It also lost two correct completions of the permitted action and two answers reporting both values. A short developer reminder prevented six unwanted writes and introduced none in its own 21 matched comparisons, but lost two permitted completions. One prevented
write came from a malformed generation, so it was not a successful completion of the task.

textRun.content: What I built and what I learned
I built a controlled agent evaluation that connects activation edits, role-probe measurements and verified actions.
I connected internal measurements to agent behavior.

I integrated role probing and activation steering into a GPT-OSS-20B agent performing a webpage-summarization task. An isolated environment and exact-content upload verification let me compare changes in the model’s activations with the actions it actually took.
I tested the intervention against controls that could challenge it.
I held pages and sampling seeds fixed across no steering, the proposed direction, its reverse and three random directions of the same magnitude. I also tested a simple instruction about the
’s permission. A zero-strength check preserved the generated tokens on identical inputs.
